(intr. py J Chu), Department of Family Medicine,
gniversity of Washington, Seattle, WA.
10 to 12 million Americans are affected by non-insulin-
dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM). NIDDM is associated
with an increased risk of hypertension and type IV
nyperlipidemia with previous studies suggesting that
cardiovascular risk factors may predict the development of
NIDDM - Past research has also shown that physical
activity helps lower lipid levels and has a protective
effect in persons at highest risk for NIDDM. We are
interested in the effect exercise has on glucose and
lipid metabolism in people with NIDDM, family history
of NIDDM, OY hyperlipidemia. We conducted a study to
determine baseline serum glucose, total cholesterol, high
density lipoprotein (HDL), low density lipoprotein (LDL),
and physical activity level in adult patients at risk for
chronic disease. Comparison of the diabetic group with the
hyperlipidemia group revealed no significant differences
in mean values of lipid, glucose, or exercise levels.
these patients did have significantly higher mean lipid
yalues than the control group. Subjects in the control
group exercised more than the patients with diabetes or
hyperlipidemia. Physical activity may help this population
of patients delay/avoid onset of chronic disease.

AND ESTABLISHED INSULIN DEPENDENT DIABETES MELLITUS. LK Wong, KL Eckert, GH
Starich, and DL Donaldson. Department of Pediatrics and Internal Medicine, University of Nevada
School of Medicine, Reno, NV
Children and adolescents with Type I diabetes mellitus (IDDM) present with a myriad of therapeutic
challenges. HbA,C is the primary indicator of long-term glycemic control. The purpose of this study was
to examine the relationship between HbA,C and the stage of IDDM (newly diagnosed (<0.1 year
duration), honeymoon (0.1-1 year duration), and established (>1 year duration)). A retrospective study of
100 children with IDDM who were under the care of a pediatric endocrinologist in a metropolitan city was
conducted. Data from 64 patients is presented. Multiple clinical indicators were examined in groups based
on both stage of IDDM and glycemic control as defined by changes in HbA,C. Delta (A) is defined as the
difference between the initial levels and the most current clinic visit. Data is reported as mean+StdDev and

DEVELOPMENT OF A SYNTHETIC PEPTIDE BASED RADIOIMMUNOASSAY FOR THE
MEASUREMENT OF MOUSE OSTEOCALCIN IN SERUM. MG Joo, VS Kadur, AK Srivastava, and
DJ Baylink, Jerry L Pettis VA Medical Center and Loma Linda University, Loma Linda, CA.
Osteocalcin is a bone specific protein secreted by osteoblasts and constitutes 1-2% of the total
bone protein. A fraction of newly synthesized osteocalcin is released into the circulation, where its
concentration reflects osteoblastic activity and rate of bone formation. Measurement of osteocalcin in
mouse serum is hampered by the tedious and cumbersome procedures involved in the purification of
osteocalcin from mouse bones. To obviate the problem of purifying large quantities of native osteocalcin
for assay development, we describe the development of a radioimmunoassay (RIA) using a synthetic
Peptide. Polyclonal antibodies were generated using a synthetic peptide conjugated to a carrier protein.
The antisera showed strong crossreactivity with intact mouse osteocalcin purified from bone. An RIA
Was developed using the synthetic peptide as the standard and calibrator. The total assay time performed
at oom temperature was four hours. Typically 5 microliters of mouse serum is required for assay, and
the sensitivity of the RIA was 0.4 nmol/L defined at 95% confidence limits. The standard curve range
Was 0.166-10.6 nmol/L. The average intraassay coefficient of variation (n 10) was <6.2%, while the
erage interassay coefficient of variation (n=4) was <13.5%, The average dilution recovery from three
scum samples (diluted up to 1:8 in assay buffer) was 98%. Correlation of the RIA with a commercially
available radioimmunoassay (that measures intact osteocalcin) using 188 mouse serum samples resulted
in 0.88 (p<0,0001). We have applied this RIA to study the remodeling that characterizes the skeletal
Phenotypes for the difference between adult peak bone density of the two strains of mice CS7BL/6J (B6)
ané C3H/HeJ (C3H), The serum osteocalcin levels were significantly greater in 8, 12, 16 and 26 week
old B6 mice, as compared to age matched C3H mice. This is consistent with the bone histomorphometric
Measurements that indicate high bone formation in C3H mice. In conclusion, we have developed an RIA
sing a synthetic peptide which shows: 1) strong crossreactivity with osteocalcin that is isolated and
Purified from mouse bone; 2) high correlation with commercially available assay with r=0.88
{P0.0001); 3) intra- and interassay CV <13.5%; and 4) that the current RIA could provide a useful tool
‘study dynamic changes in bone metabolism in the mouse model.

THE CORRELATION OF RESTING METABOLIC RATE TO FAT-FREE MASS BASED ON A
STUDY AT THE UNIVERSITY OF COLORADO NUTRITION CENTER, A. Lenny Velasquez (intr.
by J. Repine) University of Colorado Health Sciences Center, Denver, CO
This study is similar to a study done at Vanderbilt University. The Vanderbilt study looked at
the relationships between aerobic fitness level, body composition, and total daily energy expenditure.
This study differs by relating resting metabolic rate (RMR) to fat-free mass (FFM). A linear
regression equation was developed using data collected in the Energy Balance Laboratory of the

Center for Human Nutrion at the University of Colorado Health Sciences Center and compared to the
linear regression equation developed at Vanderbilt. In addition, the study facilitated a comparison of
two test methods for FFM determination. The underwater weighing method (UWW) allowed a direct
comparison to the Vanderbilt study because it was the method used at the site. The University of
Colorado Health Sciences Center Energy Balance Laboratory also uses a dual energy X-ray
absorptiometry (DEXA) method for body composition analysis. The Colorado study included 133
subjects using the UWW method and 89 subjects using the DEXA method. The Vanderbilt study
included 278 subjects. The subjects of both studies were highly heterogeneous and test protocols were
similar. The Vanderbilt study found a strong correlation between RMR and FFM. The Colorado
study also found a strong correlation. In fact, the regression equation developed at Colorado was not
significantly different to the Vanderbilt regression equation. The comparison of the UWW to the
DEXA revealed that the average DEXA reports a FFM that is .80 kilograms higher, on average, than
the average UWW. This difference represents 1.62% of the FFM values as determined by UWW.
The results of this study indicate that the correlation between RMR and FFM is the same for both the
subjects in the Vanderbuilt study and the subjects in the Colorado study. Additionally, the results find
no significant difference between UWW and the DEXA method of FFM determination.
DEVELOPMENT OF A CAT MODEL TO STUDY THE PHYSIOLOGIC RESPONSE TO THE
EXTRADURAL DEAD SPACE POST BIFRONTAL ORBITAL ADVANCEMENT JK Haslam.* HC
Nguyen, DB Kim, RA Hardesty. Intr. by Gale Starich. Department of Plastic Surgery, Loma Linda
University School of Medicine, Loma Linda, CA
Bifrontal orbital advancement (BOA) is a major surgical undertaking which can profoundly impact the
appearance of a patient with a craniofacial dysostosis. The technique of BOA leads to a large, frontal
extradural dead space (EDS). The EDS has been associated with various complications, that may involve
considerable morbidity, particularly infections.
The purpose of this study is to develop a suitable animal model to closely simulate BOA in humans with its
known associated complications and to investigate the physiological response to the EDS created. This
model differs from previous ones in that it includes the creation of bony connections between the advanced
segment of the frontal bone and the cranium, and takes into account possible infections that may occur
from the communication between the cranial and nasooropharyngeal cavities.
A cat model created by Owens and Klotch has been modified for a transcranial surgery (1993). The cats
were prepared for general anesthesia and for survival of the surgery. The procedure involves destruction
of the frontal sinus with advancement of the anterior wall and complete removal of the posterior wall,
exposing the dura mater down to the cribriform plate. Residual sinus mucosa is completely removed by 3-
minute cauterization, and sinus openings are packed with autogenous bony chips and covered with a galeal
flap. The advanced frontal bone is fixated using miniplates and titanium mesh. Occipital bone graft is
utilized to bridge the gap created as a result of the BOA, thus creating an enclosed space. A 1.5-
centimeter burr hole is made in the frontal bone to monitor the EDS response by weekly ultrasonography.

After 10 weeks, histologic sections will be viewed along with CT scans.
This study will include fifteen cats. Preliminary results demonstrate that the cats tolerate the procedure
well and sufficient ultrasound probing can provide accurate measurements of the EDS
The cat model proposed attempts to closely resemble the BOA performed in humans. This model can be
used to evaluate the physiological response to the BOA
IMMUNE SYSTEM MODULATION IN A PATIENT WITH STIFF-MAN
SYNDROME AND INSULIN-DEPENDENT DIABETES MELLITUS. DJ Walsh,
C Davis, I Hirsch, H Wei, and A Lernmark (intr. by J Chu), Departments of
Medicine and Surgery, University of Washington, Seattle, WA.
Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (IDDM) and stiff-man syndrome (SMS)
are diseases which are associated with autoimmunity. A characteristic aspect of
both IDDM and stiff-man syndrome is the presence of autoantibodies. Specifically,
autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD65) are commonly seen in
both IDDM and SMS. Using GAD6S antibody levels as a marker of the disease
process, the effects of plasmapheresis in combination with several immune system
modulators (IV IgG, mycophenolic acid, cyclophosphamide) were determined. The
modulation therapies were carried out in a 36 year old female patient who has both
IDDM and SMS. The results support the continued use of plasmapheresis in
patients with IDDM and SMS. Plasmapheresis transiently decreases antibody titers,
improves the clinical symptoms of SMS, and does not effect IDDM status.
However, the independent use of IV IgG, mycophenolic acid, and
cyclophosphamide were not found to be useful. Although the rebound of antibody
levels following plasmapheresis is significant, it is concluded from this study that
plasmapheresis is a useful treatment for patients who suffer from both IDDM and
SMS
